items.stem: To whom does Antigone speak her last farewell at the start of the scene?
options: Her friends and countrymen
Her sister and her uncle in the palace hall
The gods of Olympus
Haemon, her promised husband

items.stem: What last look does Antigone take before she goes?
options: A look at the bright sun
A look at her brother's body on the plain
A look at the palace
A look at Haemon

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “’Tis Death I _____.”
options: flee
praise
forget
wed

items.stem: To whose doomed child does Antigone compare herself?
options: Tantalus' daughter
The daughter of a Theban shepherd
Creon's wife
A priestess of Apollo

items.stem: Against what do the elders say Antigone has dashed her foot?
options: The altar of Justice
The gate of the palace
The tomb of her brother
The throne of the king of Thebes

items.stem: What does Creon order the guards to do with Antigone?
options: Shut her in a rock tomb and leave her
Take her back to her sister's room tonight
Set her free outside the city gates
Bring her before the elders for trial

items.stem: Who does Antigone hope will welcome her below?
options: Her father, mother and brother
The gods who live on Olympus
Creon's ancestors
Haemon's friends

items.stem: How does Antigone describe herself at the very end of the scene?
options: The last of the royal house
The happiest of all women in Thebes
A traitor to Thebes
A servant of Creon

items.stem: What does Antigone mean by calling herself “An alien midst the living and the dead”?
options: She belongs to neither world
She was born in a foreign city far away
She is a ghost already
She hates the living and the dead

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “Unwept, unwed, _____, hence I go”
options: crowned
honoured
unfriended
welcomed

items.stem: What do the elders say Antigone bears, in line 800?
options: Her father's guilt
Her mother's crown
Her brother's sword and shield
Creon's anger

items.stem: How does Creon claim to avoid guilt for Antigone's death?
options: She will die in the tomb, not by his hand
The gods themselves ordered the sentence on her
The elders voted for it in the council hall
Haemon agreed to it

items.stem: What does Creon say about Antigone's lament in lines 823–824?
options: It would not end if it could stop death
It moves him to change his mind at once
It is a trick taught to her by her sister
It insults the gods of Thebes

items.stem: Why does Antigone call her tomb a bridal bower?
options: It replaces the marriage she will not have
She will marry Haemon there in secret tonight
It is decorated with flowers
Creon built it for a wedding

items.stem: What tone do the elders take in lines 813–818?
options: Sympathetic but stern
Joyful and relieved
Frightened and silent
Openly rebellious against Creon

items.stem: What does Antigone's question in lines 862–864 suggest about her state of mind?
options: She feels deserted by gods and men
She is sure the gods will rescue her soon
She regrets her deed
She wants revenge on Ismene

items.stem: What does the image of Death leading Antigone to Acheron's dark fold suggest?
options: Death takes the place of her bridegroom
She will escape across the river
Death is a shepherd who cares for her
She will rule as queen in the underworld

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “The taint of blood, the hereditary _____”
options: honour
pardon
stain
treasure

items.stem: What does the triple address “O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house” emphasize?
options: Her tomb is all her future holds
She is eager to see her new home
She has made peace with Creon
She expects to be rescued before dark

items.stem: What does Antigone's reference to the “monstrous marriage-bed” recall?
options: Her parents' incestuous marriage
Her own wedding to Haemon
Creon's marriage to his wife
Polyneices' marriage in Argos to a princess

items.stem: What does Antigone mean by saying her brother's “dead hand” dealt her death-blow?
options: Burying him has led to her death
Polyneices attacked her in battle
His ghost has cursed her
His marriage ruined the family name

items.stem: What is ironic in Creon's claim to be guiltless “as concerns this maiden’s blood”?
options: He causes her death while denying responsibility
He has decided to spare her life
He admits his guilt openly
The elders have just declared him guilty before all

items.stem: What do the elders mean by “The same ungovernable will Drives like a gale the maiden still”?
options: She is as stubborn as ever
She has calmed down at last
A storm is coming to Thebes
She is trying to escape the guards

items.stem: How does Antigone's final speech appeal to Thebes?
options: She calls its gods to witness her unjust fate
She asks the people of the city to rise up against Creon
She curses the people for their silence
She begs Creon for mercy

items.stem: How does the elders' line “Thou a father’s guilt dost bear” shift the cause of her fate?
options: From her choice to an inherited curse
From the gods to Creon alone
From Creon to Haemon's love
From the curse to her sister's betrayal of the family

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “Thus by the law of _____ I was led”
options: commerce
anger
rumour
conscience

items.stem: Why is Antigone's argument in lines 849–854 often seen as troubling?
options: It seems to narrow her appeal to divine law
It shows that she did not love Polyneices
It proves that Creon's law was just
It reveals that she plans to marry

items.stem: What does Antigone's question “What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?” imply?
options: She has kept the gods' law, not broken it
She is unsure which god she offended
She admits that she broke a sacred rule
She wants the elders to name her crime

items.stem: What does Antigone's conditional wish in lines 866–869 reveal?
options: She leaves the final judgment to the gods
She has accepted that she was wrong
She curses Creon to die at once
She wants to be forgiven by the elders of Thebes

items.stem: The exchange between Antigone and the Chorus in this scene is best described as
options: A lament answered by cautious comfort and rebuke
A calm debate that ends in full agreement between them
A trial with witnesses
A prayer for the city's victory
